item.title: Neuromorphic Camera for Multi-Target Pointing Acquisition and Tracking in Free Space Optical Communication
item.description: arXiv:2611.05503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pointing, Acquisition, and Tracking (PAT) in Free-Space Optical Communication (FSOC) applications must achieve both low jitter and a large Field of View (FoV) to support beacon acquisition and multi-target tracking. While conventional frame-based sensors provide the necessary angular coverage, their performance is limited by latency, available frame-rate, and motion blur. This work explores and demonstrates the application of an event-based vision sensor for PAT tasks in FSOC. The system employs a neuromorphic sensor that asynchronously records brightness changes (events) with microsecond-level temporal resolution. The main contribution of this paper is a comparative analysis of event-based tracking algorithms for the simultaneous acquisition and tracking of multiple optical beacons that operate directly on this asynchronous stream. The performance of these strategies is validated on an experimental dataset representing realistic operational conditions for dynamic High-Altitude Platform (HAP) and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) networks. The analysis compares key metrics, such as tracking accuracy and processing latency, under various signal-to-background conditions.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Nardo, Nigitha Selvaraj, Klaus Schertler, Peter Kr\"otz, Ricardo Barrios, Sebastian Houben, Sebastian Randel

item.title: Mueller Matrix Decomposition for a General Rotating Compensator Ellipsometer
item.description: arXiv:2611.05545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work develops a Mueller matrix decomposition that factors a nondepolarizing Mueller matrix $M$ into three components $M = T_1 D T_2$, where the elements $D$, which correspond to a diagonal Jones matrix, are separated from rotations and circular diattenuation $T_1, T_2$. This decomposition is employed to calibrate a prototype reflective rotating-compensator ellipsometer designed to operate using extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation. This decomposition allows for the measurement of the full Mueller matrix of a sample without full knowledge of the compensators or the source polarization, while allowing for significant diattenuation and retardance for the optics. A generalization of the decomposition is developed for depolarizing Mueller matrices, and the technique is tested on reflection data collected on an Au mirror at $266$ nm.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Chew, Purnima P. Balakrishnan, Bryan M. Barnes, John H. Burnett, Colton K. Dudley, Steven E. Grantham, Stephanie L. Moffitt, Charles Tarrio, Thomas A. Germer

item.title: A closed-form design rule for photonic hopfions of arbitrary order
item.description: arXiv:2611.05595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological textures of light are robust against perturbation and are emerging as carriers of information and probes of light-matter interaction. The most intricate of them, the photonic hopfion, in which the loops of different polarization states are linked, has so far been assembled from chosen superpositions of laser modes, with weights set by hand or found by numerical optimization. Here we replace this search with a design rule. Two scalar beams, an optical vortex of order $\ell$ and a field with n dark rings, propagate in closed form, and their phases on one plane are the two masks of a metasurface that controls two orthogonal polarizations. Although a beam, unlike the closed spaces of topology, extends to infinity, we prove that it is a hopfion of order $n\ell$ whenever three algebraic conditions on the ring coefficients and the vortex order hold, and that the polarization loops of every state that the far field does not reach then link exactly $n\ell$ times; each condition guards against one way in which the topology can escape. The order is thus chosen on paper and the device follows directly, without optimization. In scalar simulation, one terahertz metasurface geometry produces hopfions up to order nine, and a full-wave simulation of the complete first-order device preserves its topology. The rule applies to any platform that shapes the phases of two orthogonal polarizations.
item.dc:creator: Ali Nadarloo, Mohammad Javad Hajiahmadi, Mohammad Soleimani

item.title: Time-resolved infrared spectroscopy with entangled photons and visible-light detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.05800v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-resolved infrared (TR-IR) spectroscopy reveals molecular structural changes and charge-carrier dynamics on their intrinsic timescales, in photosynthesis, catalysis and optoelectronic materials, but requires complex sources of ultrashort infrared pulses, cryogenically cooled detectors to overcome thermal background, and intense probes that can perturb the sample. Quantum infrared spectroscopy avoids these constraints: harnessing quantum interference between the generation processes of frequency-entangled photon pairs, it reads out the infrared response of a sample by detecting only the visible partner photon, for which efficient detectors exist. To date, it has been limited to steady-state measurements. Here we demonstrate its ultrafast, time-resolved form with a picosecond visible pump pulse and a silicon detector. Each visible pulse generates photon pairs within a picosecond window; the infrared photon of a pair probes the excited sample at a set delay after excitation, and the transient response is read out from the count rate of its visible partner. We resolve picosecond carrier dynamics in a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror near 1529 nm with a picowatt-level probe, unaffected by thermal background and by sample IR photoluminescence 50 times stronger than the probe. The approach is applicable to the mid-infrared, fingerprint region, where infrared detection is hardest, and to the terahertz region.
item.dc:creator: Jasleen Kaur, Yu Mukai, Ryo Okamoto, Shigeki Takeuchi

item.title: Optical angular momentum and pseudospin-orbit coupling in photonic graphene
item.description: arXiv:2611.05944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the dynamics of structured laser beams carrying angular momentum (AM) as they undergo conical diffraction in photonic graphene. Using a combination of numerical simulations and analytical calculations, we demonstrate a surprising result: the beam's orbital AM tracks the dynamics of the lattice pseudospin rather than the AM of its slowly varying envelope. This finding provides evidence that pseudospin behaves as a genuine form of angular momentum. Furthermore, we explore beam propagation in staggered honeycomb lattices governed by the massive Dirac equation, revealing that the orbital AM is highly sensitive to both the band gap size and the envelope's initial AM. We explain our numerical results by drawing an analogy with the orbital magnetization of electrons.
item.dc:creator: Omri Bahat-Treidel, Daniel Leykam, Anton S. Desyatnikov

item.title: Single-sided lens terahertz flat-top beam shaping in the Fresnel region
item.description: arXiv:2611.06050v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, a novel, to our knowledge, analytical approach is introduced for the design of a single-sided plano-convex lens (PCL) capable of terahertz (THz) flat-top beam shaping in the Fresnel region. The lens profile, derived from geometrical optics principles, integrates collimating and beam-shaping functions into a single optical surface, thereby simplifying fabrication. The efficiency of the method is demonstrated by designing two PCLs that convert a divergent Gaussian beam from a monochromatic THz source (at 100 and 200 GHz) into flat-top beams with target radii of 400 and 500 mm at distances of 3 and 4 m, respectively. The resulting fields, evaluated through analytical, integral equation, and finite element techniques, are shown to be comparable to those produced by a conventional double-sided concave-convex lens. Furthermore, the sensitivity of the design to frequency and alignment variations is investigated, confirming the robustness of this single-curvature approach for integration into practical THz imaging systems.
item.dc:creator: Ehsan Imanbeygi, Mohammad Hossein Koohi Ghamsari, Mehdi Ahmadi-Boroujeni, Babak Honarbakhsh

item.title: Millimeter-Wave Gaussian-to-Flat-Top Beam Shaping Using a Single-Curvature Lens: A Novel Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.06053v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a novel method for converting the divergent Gaussian intensity distribution of a millimeter-wave source into a uniform (flat-top) distribution using a single curved surface. The proposed method combines the surface profile of a collimator with that of a beam shaper. To validate the method, the profile of a single-sided (plano-convex) lens is derived and placed 52 mm in front of a conical horn antenna operating at 100 GHz. The lens transforms the Gaussian radiation of the horn, with an incident beam radius of 11.9 mm, into a uniform beam with a radius of 400 mm at a distance of 3 m. The lens surface profile is optimized using a full-wave-simulation-based procedure, and the resulting output beam is compared with that of a previously designed double-sided (concave-convex) lens. Simulation results show that, within the desired field of view, the optimized single-sided lens produces a flat-top intensity distribution with satisfactory ripple and roll-off. Finally, the sensitivity of the optimized lens to frequency variation is investigated. The proposed lens is suitable for generating uniform illumination in active stand-off millimeter-wave imaging systems.
item.dc:creator: Ehsan Imanbeygi, Mohammad Hossein Koohi Ghamsari, Mehdi Ahmadi-Boroujeni

item.title: Colloidal 2D WS2 nanosheets exhibiting high-purity single photon emission
item.description: arXiv:2611.06144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The search for quantum emitters, delivering single photons "on demand" at cryogenic and elevated temperatures for photonic technologies is ever progressing. For example, micrometer-sized WS2 monolayers exhibit single photon emission by elaborated local defect or strain engineering. Here, we show that wet-chemically synthesised monolayered two-dimensional (2D) WS2 nano sheets (NSs) with lateral sizes of 14 (+/- 6 nm) readily emit single photons from exciton recombination without the need for substrate-induced patterning, strain/defect engineering or spectral filtering. Single particle spectroscopy of 70 individual NSs shows photoluminescence from excitons (2.02 eV), trios (1.94 eV) and defect-localized states (1.85 eV) with fast emission (t1<0.2 ns, t2=3.2 ns), allowing highly frequent excitation cycles. Pulsed at 80 MHz, colloidal WS2 NSs exhibit limited spectral diffusion, no blinking and distinct photon antibunching (g2(0)=0.07 at 5 K), thereby tackling challenges of established colloidal quantum dot systems (blinking, longer emission cycles), while retaining high single photon purity as key quality of deterministic quantum emitters.
item.dc:creator: Markus Xemaire, Jakob Keck, Marco K\"ogel, Marc Brecht, Jannik C. Meyer, Alfred J. Meixner, Jannika Lauth

item.title: BIC-Engineered Silicon Nitride Microring Resonators Enabled by an Etch-Free Laser-Writing Approach
item.description: arXiv:2611.06167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report the initial experimental demonstration of a complementary, etch-free approach with fewer fabrication steps, in useful SU-8 ridges written by direct ultraviolet laser lithography on an unpatterned silicon nitride film define waveguides and microring resonators. Because the nitride film is never patterned, scattering at patterned nitride sidewalls does not arise, and the remaining radiative loss is engineered by design. The guided transverse-magnetic mode lies within the continuum of transverse-electric slab modes, and we use bound states in the continuum (BICs) as a design tool to control this radiation. Coupled-mode analysis and full-vectorial simulations show that radiation from the two ridge sidewalls cancels by destructive interference at discrete widths, with a first BIC at 2.25 micron and radiation below 1 dB/cm over a 0.3 micron width window and about 200 nm of bandwidth, and that curvature confines this cancellation to discrete bands of bending radius and width. Laser-written waveguides follow the predicted width dependence of the loss, reaching approximately 1.5 dB/cm near the BIC, where non-radiative loss dominates. A microring designed on a radius-selected BIC band exhibits loaded quality factors up to 1.6 \times 10^4 and, under the over-coupled assignment supported by a coupler model, an intrinsic quality factor of 3.3 \times 10^5. Because radiation is set by a patterned low-index layer on an unetched film, the same approach could be extended to other nanostructures. Optimization of the writing conditions and materials is ongoing.
item.dc:creator: Leila Hajshahvaladi, Mohammad Amin Salmani, Media Abbasi, Mobin Yaghoobi, Mohammad Asgari, Gholam-Mohammad Parsanasab

item.title: Closed-form dyadic Green functions for transversely uniaxial bianisotropic medium with equal magnetoelectric scalars
item.description: arXiv:2611.06172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A transversely uniaxial bianisotropic medium with equal magnetoelectric scalars was conceived by Weiglhofer in 1994. Using the scalar factorization method, he concluded that the dyadic Green functions of this medium could not be found in closed form. That conclusion is incorrect. The essentials of the derivation are reproduced here, and closed-form expressions are given for all four dyadic Green functions of the unbounded medium, linking the electric and magnetic fields to electric and magnetic source current densities.
item.dc:creator: Akhlesh Lakhtakia (The Pennsylvania State University), Tom G. Mackay (University of Edinburgh)

item.title: Spatial structure of surface plasmon resonance under narrow-beam illumination and its implications for sensing
item.description: arXiv:2611.06222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The reflection of light on a surface plasmon resonance structure can be understood as the interference between the direct Fresnel reflection and the light radiated back by the plasmon as it propagates along the metal film. When the beam waist is only an order of magnitude larger than the surface plasmon propagation length, these two contributions separate spatially, and their destructive interference localizes into a dark fringe within the reflected beam. We develop an analytical model of this effect, design a realistic setup based on off-the-shelf components to observe it, and simulate the complete experiment, from illumination to detection, with an open-source framework. In the regime where the interference is maximized, the spatial structure of the reflected beam becomes extremely sensitive to the outer medium. This allows us to define an observable more than an order of magnitude more sensitive than amplitude-based measurements, and we expect a comparable improvement in resolution.
item.dc:creator: Tristan Miralles, R\'emi Poll\`es, Pauline Bennet, Denis Langevin, Martine Mihailovic, Emmanuel Centeno, Jack Mock, David R. Smith, Antoine Moreau

item.title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2611.06240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}\lambda^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.
item.dc:creator: Stavros Athanasiou, Olivier J. F. Martin, Francisco J. Garc\'ia-Vidal, Johannes Feist

item.title: A Design Rule for Passive Reconfigurable Microwave Devices
item.description: arXiv:2611.06279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every reconfigurable microwave device places a tuning element - a varactor, a diode, transistor, microelectromechanical or phase-change switch, a ferroelectric or liquid-crystal load - inside a fixed passive network. The network can make a small change of the element produce a large change of the response, and design practice often credits it with the device's tuning capability. This paper shows that a fixed, linear, passive network cannot add to that capability. Each tuning element carries a tuning budget, a dimensionless length computed from its own impedance trajectory, and a fixed passive network can transmit that budget or lose part of it, never enlarge it. The unit of the budget is the hyperbolic distance of the Smith chart: the distance from a match is the logarithm of the voltage standing-wave ratio, and the distance between two states sets their mutual mismatch and is the logarithm of their commutation quality factor. From one inequality we derive closed-form, ready-to-use limits for analog and digital phase shifters, true-time-delay lines, switches, attenuators, vector modulators, impedance tuners, tunable filters, reconfigurable antennas, metasurface cells and multiport networks; the two-state and attenuation limits are attained by explicit circuits, and the phase limit by a constant-loss trajectory. We introduce the $\Lambda$-chart, a Smith-chart companion on which budgets and requirements are read graphically, and apply it to four published microwave case studies.
item.dc:creator: Ali Nadarloo, Mohammad Javad Hajiahmadi, Mohammad Soleimani

item.title: Evanescent-Depth-Engineered High-Q topological Cavities for Strong Photon-Exciton Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2611.06351v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Due to the inherent scattering in topological edge states, the topological resonant cavity (TRC) formed by their interference exhibits a relatively low quality factor (Q). To address this issue, we propose the mechanism of engineering the transverse evanescent depth of edge states to achieve high-Q in irregular shaped TRCs, which further enables strong photon-exciton coupling at the single-quantum level. By adjusting the intra- and inter-cell coupling strengths in the pseudo-spin topological photonic crystal, the transverse evanescent depth of edge states is greatly reduced, thereby suppressing the scattering of TRCs. Consequently, the Q of various shaped TRCs with 2 ~ 3 um size is up to 10^5 ~ 10^6 in the visible, so that the strong photon-exciton coupling is achieved. The high-Q topological cavities hold promising application in integrated lasers, sensors, cavity quantum electrodynamics, and quantum photonics.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Mo, Renxuan Peng, Haoyang Zhang, Yu Tian, Ying Gu

item.title: Directional Control of Chiral Polymer Emission Dissymmetry by Plasmonic Metasurfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.06400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Circularly polarized (CP) emission is central to next-generation photonic and optoelectronic technologies, yet simultaneously controlling its directionality, intensity, and handedness remains a major challenge. Advances in molecular and materials design have enabled strong chiral light-matter interactions and large dissymmetry between opposite CP states. However, conventional thin-film architectures provide limited control over the angular distribution of CP emission and often exhibit strongly angle-dependent chiral emission. Metasurfaces, on the other hand, offer powerful control over emission directionality and polarization, but have predominantly been explored with intrinsically achiral emitters. For the first time, we integrate organic chiral polymer thin films with planar chiral plasmonic metasurfaces to enhance chiral light-matter interactions while controlling the directionality and angular dependence of chiral emission. Using angle-resolved Stokes Fourier polarimetry, we show that metasurface coupling produces directional emission, near-normal dissymmetry factors exceeding 0.7, and, remarkably, direction-dependent reversal of the emission handedness at fixed molecular stereochemistry.
item.dc:creator: Debapriya Pal, Louis Minion, David Reger, Jessica Wade, Matthew J. Fuchter, A. Femius Koenderink

item.title: Phase matching and mode coupling in photonic-crystal ring resonators
item.description: arXiv:2611.06456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic-crystal ring resonators, in which periodic refractive-index modulations couple counter-propagating modes, have become a widely used platform for nonlinear photonics, offering mode-by-mode dispersion engineering. When several modulation components are superimposed, their relative angular alignment (phase) is an additional degree of freedom whose impact on the nonlinear dynamics has remained unclear. Here we show that the relative phases between the modulation patterns have a decisive impact. Through the interference of the nonlinear processes in forward and backward direction, they add a phase and mode selection rule to the established phase-matching conditions, which can fully suppress nonlinear coupling. They also impose a relative spectral chirp between forward- and backward-propagating waveforms. We illustrate these effects for parametric oscillation and dissipative Kerr solitons. Our results extend the concept of phase matching to resonators with interfering nonlinear pathways and establish the alignment of index gratings as a design dimension for nonlinear microresonators.
item.dc:creator: Alexander E. Ulanov, Lukas Bengel, Tobias Herr

item.title: Geometric Pumping of Optical Work in Coherent Wave Scattering
item.description: arXiv:2611.06666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical work exchanged between light and time-varying matter underlies a wide range of emerging photonic technologies, yet a general geometric theory describing its generation and control has been lacking. Here we establish such a theory for coherent electromagnetic scattering. We show that the net optical work accumulated during an adiabatic modulation cycle is a geometric quantity determined by the Berry curvature of the outgoing field in parameter space. Nonzero optical work can thus be generated by cyclically modulating two or more independent system parameters. In contrast to conventional adiabatic pumping between incoherent reservoirs, optical work pumping vanishes under maximally mixed illumination. Greater illumination coherence increases the maximum work attainable through wavefront shaping. For fully coherent illumination, we derive the optimal incident wavefront and modulation trajectory that maximize the optical work per cycle. Our framework unifies time-varying photonics, optomechanics, and geometric transport within a common scattering formalism.
item.dc:creator: Zeyu Kuang, Konstantin Y. Bliokh, Stefan Rotter

item.title: Photonic and Electronic Interaction of TMD-Hybridized ZnO Nanowire Lasers
item.description: arXiv:2611.06740v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semiconductor nanowire lasers are promising on-chip coherent light sources for photonic integrated circuits, but integration inevitably places them in contact with other materials, thereby changing their properties upon hybridization. In this study, we examine the photonic and electronic coupling between single ZnO nanowire lasers and TMDs. Using deterministic nanomanipulation, we first hybridized the same nanowire first with a WS$_2$ monolayer and then with a MoS$_2$ monolayer. The respective lasing threshold rises, the emission is strongly quenched at high pump power densities, and the mode envelope blueshifts. Upon hybridization with bilayer, trilayer, and bulk MoS$_2$, lasing is fully suppressed. Finite-Difference Eigenmode simulations show that the TMD absorbs part of the evanescent field. Because this absorption is wavelength dependent, it also removes modes from the low-energy flank of the envelope, which accounts for small difference between the two monolayers, while the blueshift itself follows the increase of the carrier density at threshold. Density functional theory calculations that include the interface dipole predict a type-I alignment at the ideal ZnO(10$\bar{1}$0)/TMD interface, which turns into type~II for a moderately reduced dipole, as expected for hydroxylated facets in air. In both cases, holes are transferred from the nanowire into the TMD and removed from the gain medium. Evanescent absorption and hole transfer thus jointly suppress lasing, and both must be accounted for when integrating nanowire lasers with 2D materials.
item.dc:creator: Moritz Willems, Edwin Eobaldt, Alexander Zaunick, Aurelia Eberhard, Maximilian Tomoscheit, Lukas Raam J\"ager, Xiao Chen, Preeti Sharma, Nicolas Tancogne-Dejean, Antony George, Andrey Turchanin, Silvana Botti, Giancarlo Soavi, Carsten Ronning

item.title: 3D Printed Monolithic Optomechanical Chassis for an Unbalanced Field-Widened Interferometer
item.description: arXiv:2611.06898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Additive manufacturing is increasingly being explored as an approach for producing complex structures for optical hardware. In this work, we present a fully monolithic optomechanical chassis fabricated using laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing. The structure was fabricated from thermally stable Invar36, a low-thermal-expansion alloy that enables high dimensional stability under varying environmental conditions. Our monolithic design incorporates embedded optical mounts, flexures, and alignment features directly into the chassis geometry that exceed the practical limits of conventional subtractive manufacturing. By integrating the optomechanical support structure into a single compact unit, the system achieves a reduced footprint compared to traditional optomechanical assemblies. The results demonstrate the potential of additive manufacturing to produce lightweight, and highly customized optical systems, opening the possibility of new pathways for next-generation quantum sensors and optical instrumentation.
item.dc:creator: Ramy Tannous, Dogan Sinar, Sagar Patel, Tabitha D. Arulpragasam, Issa Rishmawi, Mark Kirby, Vlad Paserin, Mihaela Vlasea, Thomas Jennewein

item.title: Collectively pumped superradiant laser with coherence scaling beyond the standard quantum limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.05976v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For more than half a century, the standard quantum limit (SQL) was thought to limit the laser coherence $\mathfrak{C}$ -- the number of photons emitted from the laser into the beam in one coherence time -- to a scaling $\Theta(\mu^2)$, where $\mu$ is the mean number of optical-frequency excitations stored inside the laser. However, recently it has been shown [Baker et al., Nat. Phys. 17, 179 (2021)] that the Heisenberg limit -- an achievable ultimate limit set by quantum mechanics for the task of producing a beam with the standard properties of a laser beam -- is $\mathfrak{C}=\Theta(\mu^4)$, a quadratic enhancement. So far, proposals to demonstrate beyond-SQL scaling of $\mathfrak{C}$ have been limited to circuit QED, at microwave frequencies (i.e., a maser). Here, we introduce a class of generalized far-above-threshold (FAT) laser models, obtained by replacing the ordinary bosonic lowering operator $\hat{a}$ by a general lowering operator $\hat{L}$ in the superoperators appearing in the master equation that governs the FAT laser dynamics. We then show that an optical-frequency superradiant laser in the bad-cavity limit, with feedback-controlled collective pumping, realizes one such model, in which $\hat{L}$ is identified with the collective superradiant lowering operator $\hat{J}$. This model can surpass the SQL scaling, with the coherence exhibiting a scaling as large as $\mathfrak{C}= \Theta(\mu^{8/3})$ in the optimal parameter regime. Here, in the bad-cavity limit, $\mu\approx N/2$, where $N$ is the number of superradiant atoms.
item.dc:creator: Ori Somech, Howard M. Wiseman

item.title: Perturbation-Based Reconstruction of Depth-Resolved OCT Attenuation without Requiring a Fully Decayed Signal Tail
item.description: arXiv:2611.05983v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Depth-resolved attenuation in optical coherence tomography (OCT) can provide quantitative optical contrast beyond structural imaging. However, conventional reconstruction methods can be biased when the OCT signal does not fully decay within the imaging range or when the distal signal tail is dominated by noise or residual reflections from distal sample or support interfaces. Here, we present a perturbation-based Beer-Lambert framework that combines a zeroth-order exponential estimate with a first-order correction, reducing reliance on the unreliable distal signal tail below the current depth. Numerical A-line simulations, Monte Carlo modeling, multilayer silicone-dye-TiO2 phantoms, and ex vivo bovine retina experiments were used to evaluate the method under finite-depth and heterogeneous imaging conditions. The numerical A-line tests showed reduced depth-dependent error against prescribed attenuation profiles; the Monte Carlo comparisons showed less distal drift relative to model-defined benchmarks, while the phantom profiles were compared with separately acquired single-layer OCT calibration values. In a Monte Carlo component test that withheld vessel-mask and vessel-boundary information from reconstruction and used that information only for post hoc evaluation, the first-order correction recovered 61% of the segmentation-informed target vessel contrast and reduced vessel ROI mean absolute error by 65% relative to the fixed zeroth-order baseline. These results suggest that perturbation-based reconstruction may provide a practical approach for depth-resolved reconstruction of effective OCT attenuation when the fully decayed A-line condition is not satisfied.
item.dc:creator: Jinglun Yu, Yaning Wang, Shuwen Wei, Jin U. Kang

item.title: Free electrons unveil nanolaser physics at the sub-picosecond and nanometer scale
item.description: arXiv:2603.23237v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Semiconducting nanowire lasers (NWLs) constitute nanoscale modular and tunable light sources, essential components for integrated optoelectronics. However, advancing NWL operation requires characterization of their near-field and dynamics at the nanometer scale, which is hampered by the diffraction limit of light. Here, we show a non-perturbative measurement of the absolute number of photons in a GaN/InGaN nanowire nanolaser cavity above the lasing threshold with sub-picosecond resolution and maps of the lasing mode spatial profile at the nanoscale. For this we use photon-induced near-field electron microscopy while simultaneously measuring the photons far-field, unraveling the key nanoscale and time-resolved characteristics of a NWL in operation. With this technique, we observed lasing with a pump-power-dependent time offset of 0.5-1 ps that reflects carrier thermalization and spontaneous emission, and a pulse duration of 500 to 700 fs. From the spatial maps of the lasing mode, we observe TM-polarized azimuthal whispering gallery modes along the nanowire circumference, as well as two distinct Fabry-Perot modes along the nanowire length. These spatial maps allow us to understand which of the multiple complex cavity modes available in the nanowire are responsible for lasing paving the way for their practical application into devices.
item.dc:creator: Cl\'eo Santini, Thi Huong Ngo, Luiz H. G. Tizei, Aur\'elie Lloret, Tom Fraysse, Sebastien Weber, Adrien Teurtrie, Albert Polman, Virginie Br\"andli, Sebastien Chenot, Denis Lefebvre, St\'ephane V\'ezian, Hugo Louren\c{c}o-Martins, Christelle Brimont, Benjamin Damilano, Thierry Guillet, Sophie Meuret

item.title: Leaky-Wave Antenna Analysis using Multi-Modal Network Theory with Open Periodic Boundaries
item.description: arXiv:2604.17571v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces two methods for analyzing periodic leaky-wave antennas (LWAs) within a new framework denoted as multi-modal network theory (MNT) with open periodic boundaries (OPBs). The approach is hybrid, combining analytical techniques with a commercial full-wave solver. The first method computes the dispersion diagram of periodic LWAs. It is iterative and relies on the full-wave simulation of a single unit cell of a LWA, coupled with the analytical solution of an eigenvalue problem. This method effectively captures both the phase and attenuation constants of periodic LWAs while using fewer modes than previous methods with commercial frequency-domain solvers. The method is validated by computing the dispersion of classic LWA unit cells and comparing them to those obtained through full-wave simulations of the full-length antenna and other state-of-the-art methods. The second, also based on OPB-MNT, focuses on LWA driven analysis. Specifically, it determines the response of a unit cell to an incident plane wave. To validate this method, we compute the response of LWAs with different unit cell designs. By comparing these results with the corresponding dispersion analysis, we highlight the differences between the driven case and eigenvalue problems and identify the scenarios in which the former is applicable.
item.dc:creator: Oscar Senlis, John N. Le, Anthony Grbic, Mauro Ettorre, Vincent Laquerbe, David Gonz\'alez-Ovejero

item.title: Harnessing Machine Learning for Ultrafast Science in Facility Settings: Opportunities and Challenges
item.description: arXiv:2610.12146v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Ultrafast science is rapidly evolving from a collection of specialized laser experiments into a facility-scale, data-intensive research endeavour. High-repetition-rate femtosecond and attosecond sources, synchronized multidimensional diagnostics, and increasingly nonlinear laser-matter interactions now generate heterogeneous data streams whose volume, speed, and complexity often exceed the capacity of conventional manual workflows. This chapter examines how machine learning can become an enabling layer for next-generation ultrafast facilities, with emphasis on the Extreme Light Infrastructure (ELI) ecosystem. We discuss the scientific drivers for artificial-intelligence-assisted experimentation, propose a facility-scale digital architecture spanning acquisition, ingestion, storage, analytics, machine learning, adaptive feedback, and user interfaces, and review representative examples from ELI ALPS, ELI Beamlines, and ELI-NP. The central thesis is that machine learning should not be treated merely as an offline data-analysis tool; rather, when constrained by physical insight and embedded in robust data infrastructure, it can support real-time diagnostics, surrogate modeling, anomaly detection, experimental optimization, and progressively autonomous discovery workflows.
item.dc:creator: Mousumi Upadhyay Kahaly, Ishraq Md Anjum, Davorin Peceli, Zsolt Diveki, Subhendu Kahaly

item.title: Unified Theory of Spin and Orbital Inverse Faraday Effects in Rashba Metals
item.description: arXiv:2603.13187v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The inverse Faraday effect (IFE) offers a promising route toward optical control of magnetic moments in quantum materials. Yet experiments on spin-orbit-coupled metals indicate that no single microscopic mechanism suffices, implicating orbital currents alongside spin polarization. We derive both responses in a disordered Rashba metal using quantum kinetics and diagrammatics with impurity-renormalized optical vertices, providing the first unified diagrammatic derivation of spin and orbital IFE. Treating impurity scattering consistently, our number-conserving kinetic formulation restores full phase-space derivatives and the optical magnetic field neglected in earlier treatments. We connect nonlinear orbital magnetization to absorptive linear optical conductivity, revealing that the magnetic Lorentz force supplies half the orbital response. Our unified treatment resolves both channels across the Rashba resonance: spin IFE changes sign as frequency increases, while the orbital IFE dominates, keeping the direction of the total magnetization unchanged.
item.dc:creator: Jaglul Hasan, Maxim Dzero, Chandan Setty

item.title: Squeezing Enhancement Through Resonant Interference in Multi-ring Resonators
item.description: arXiv:2605.10731v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a non-perturbative description of squeezed light generation in an arbitrary lossy structure consisting of multiple coupled microring resonators. This is applied to two ring photonic molecules where the interference of the fields in the coupled rings leads to a modification in the resonance spectrum near a shared resonance. Considering a dual-pump degenerate squeezing scheme under a five resonance approximation, we investigate two methods to suppress parasitic four-wave mixing contributions and compensate for group velocity dispersion within a primary resonator through hybridization effects with a second auxiliary resonator. In the former case, this comes from an effective splitting of the unwanted resonances supporting parasitic four-wave mixing interactions that add thermal noise to the desired degenerate squeezed state. For sufficiently strong coupling between the resonators, we demonstrate near complete suppression of such parasitic processes, resulting in near unit fidelities with the corresponding output state that would arise were the parasitic interactions neglected. In the latter case, the hybridization effectively shifts a pump resonance, realigning the desired dual-pump four-wave mixing process and leading to a significant enhancement of the signal generation and output squeezing.
item.dc:creator: M. Sloan, J. E. Sipe

item.title: Attosecond delay metrology beyond the photon coherence time with spectrally resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry
item.description: arXiv:2607.16849v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry enables delay estimation at the quantum precision limit but is traditionally constrained to path differences within the coherence time of the interfering photons. Here, we demonstrate single-shot path-delay sensing using spectrally resolved HOM interference, achieving a precision near the measurement Cram\'er-Rao bound over an operating range of approximately $\pm$300 um, removing the conventional dynamic-range limitation imposed by the photon coherence window. By extracting delay information from the spectral interference fringes of spectrally entangled photon pairs, we retain near-optimal sensitivity over an operational range exceeding the photon coherence time by over two orders of magnitude. Using one million detected photon pairs, we achieve a time-delay precision of 13 attosecond (4 nm), while real-time operation (at 1 Hz) with 2000 detected photons yields 330 attosecond (100 nm) precision. Because the estimator relies on fringe periodicity rather than absolute coincidence rates, the method is intrinsically robust to variations in interference visibility, eliminating the need for recalibration. As a practical demonstration, we measure the thickness of a nominally 300 um transmissive target with nanometer-scale precision. These results mark a significant step towards deploying quantum-enhanced HOM interferometry for high-precision displacement sensing in real-world applications.
item.dc:creator: Yingwen Zhang, Kyle Jordan, Duncan England, Vincenzo Tamma, Ebrahim Karimi, Benjamin Sussman

item.title: Quantum Magnonics: Quantum States Generation and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2607.27771v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hybrid systems based on magnons in ferromagnetic materials, such as yttrium iron garnet, have achieved remarkable development in the last decade. These include the coupling of magnons to microwave and optical photons, superconducting qubits, phonons, spins, the center-of-mass motion of a ferromagnet, etc. Here, we review both the experimental and theoretical progress in this field, focusing on the generation of magnonic quantum states and their applications in a broad range of fields. Since the strong coupling is a prerequisite for achieving coherent quantum control of magnons and preparing magnonic quantum states, we start by introducing representative strong-coupling experiments in cavity magnonics, then review a series of protocols for creating various magnonic quantum states, such as Fock, cat, squeezed, and entangled states, and discuss their potential applications in macroscopic quantum studies, quantum information science, quantum sensing, magnonic quantum devices, dark matter detection, and so on. Finally, we summarize the review and give an outlook for the future study of quantum magnonics.
item.dc:creator: Zi-Xu Lu, Xuan Zuo, Xin-Lei Hei, Gang Liu, Zeng-Xing Liu, Qi Guo, Peng-Bo Li, Jie Li

item.title: Multimode Angle-Compensated Interferometer with Long Time-Bin Delay Using a Multi-Pass Herriott Cell
item.description: arXiv:2608.13399v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interference of optical signals in free-space channels requires optical receivers to support many spatial modes due to atmospheric turbulence, typically necessitating adaptive optics systems. Angle-compensated interferometers offer a passive alternative, making them particularly attractive for time-bin encoded signals with delays on the order of one nanosecond. Here, we demonstrate a multimode angle-compensated interferometer design that achieves a high interference visibility for spatially multimode beams with large time bin separations. The interference of the multimode beams is enabled using an imaging multi-pass Herriott cell that enables a very long path separation with a small form-factor. The design is tested using both numerical ray-tracing simulations and proof-of-principle demonstrations. We create a prototype interferometer with a path length difference of 12ns and determine that it maintains a high interference visibility with a large field-of-view of $0.4^{\circ}$.
item.dc:creator: Ramy Tannous, St\'ephane Vinet, Kaylee Sherk, Kimia Mohammadi, Thomas Jennewein

item.title: Negative quasiprobabilities redistribute (and complex ones reduce) the information in unabsorbed photons
item.description: arXiv:2610.00740v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Negative Kirkwood--Dirac quasiprobabilities are credited with the quantum advantage of interaction-free measurement and postselected metrology. We test that claim on the task interaction-free measurement was designed for: learning about a sample while it absorbs as little light as possible. The quasiprobability distribution of path and output gives the linear response to a weak sample: its real part responds to absorption, its imaginary part to a phase. For a pure single photon passing once through any interferometer, the Fisher information about transmittance per absorbed photon is the direct-transmission value minus a sum of squared imaginary parts: no interferometer or readout beats direct transmission. Negativity only concentrates information in weakly lit outputs. These imaginary parts depend on the output basis, not the sample, so an optimal basis with all terms real always exists. A single photon beats direct transmission only through a phase response, which for an optical line needs a thick or inhomogeneously broadened sample, or through many passes when absorptions go uncounted, as a critically coupled resonator shows. For detecting a weak absorber, negativity gives a single-shot advantage that does not accumulate over repeated trials. The advantage that accumulates comes from outputs dark without the object, and needs no negativity.
item.dc:creator: Jonte R. Hance

item.title: Optimal linear-optical interferometers for unitary t-designs in a multi-photon Fock space
item.description: arXiv:2610.12646v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the construction of unitary \(1\)-designs and two-photon designs on programmable linear-optical interferometers. Using the frame-potential loss as the optimization objective, we identify architectures that reproduce the relevant Haar moments with considerably fewer programmable phase shifters than required for universal linear optics. For unitary \(1\)-designs, we provide an exact construction and prove that the minimum number of programmable phase shifters within the considered layered architecture is \(2(d-1)\), where \(d\) is the number of optical modes. Numerical optimization confirms this parameter count over the tested range of dimensions. For two-photon designs, defined by first-moment matching in the symmetric two-photon representation of \(U(d)\), we numerically investigate the resources required to achieve prescribed approximation thresholds. We benchmark the resulting ensembles using single- and two-photon transition probabilities and average channel fidelities. Furthermore, we develop a protocol for estimating the total photon number of a multiphoton Fock state using a single monitored output mode and derive the corresponding Haar-averaged photon-count moments. Our findings demonstrate that shallow interferometers can reproduce Haar-averaged observables with reduced hardware resources, while photon-number fluctuations provide a more stringent test of approximate two-photon designs.
item.dc:creator: Robert A. Grinshtein, Ivan V. Dyakonov, Stanislav S. Straupe

item.title: Pump-scheme dependence of few-emitter lasers: exact multilevel correlations and photon statistics
item.description: arXiv:2611.01205v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Few-emitter laser models usually replace the excitation cycle of the gain medium by a single Markovian pump jump of a two-level emitter. We test this replacement with the cavity and laser-transition parameters held fixed and the two-level pump rate fitted to the same mean photon number, using an exact damping-basis continued-fraction solution of the cavity--emitter master equation for $N$ identical $d$-level emitters with arbitrary independent incoherent transitions and one cavity-coupled transition, in the known reduced space of level populations and lasing coherences. First, a pump-quantum filtration shows that the inter-emitter coherence of $\Lambda$ and ladder media starts at second rather than first order in the pump; we evaluate its leading coefficient from the exact finite-system series and map the recycling rate at which its sign changes. Second, at matched photon number, rate-limited steps in the pump cycle push the long-time output-counting Fano factor of two and three emitters well below one: for two emitters it reaches 0.66 at a mean cavity occupation of 0.3 and is still 0.74 at an occupation of one, where $g^{(2)}(0)$ is within 3% of unity, because the anticorrelation sits at delays of about half a cavity lifetime rather than at zero delay. For two and three emitters the fitted two-level model gets both statistics wrong and places the output above the shot-noise level. Against independent single-emitter lasers at the same output, the common cavity erodes rather than enhances this single-emitter effect.
item.dc:creator: Stephan Hartmann

item.title: Reading Why: Born-Measured Attention with Exact Word Evidence on Light and Qubits
item.description: arXiv:2611.05355v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a language model answers, we can usually only estimate why. We build a transformer in which every step is a Born measurement - attention $|\langle q|k\rangle|^4$ normalised over each row, a measured product in place of the feed-forward nonlinearity, and a Born readout. With its denominators held at their values for the input, each class probability is a polynomial in the word amplitudes, so its integrated-gradient evidence is computed by a finite quadrature with no quadrature error: the words' contributions sum to the class probability above its no-information share, to $10^{-11}$ or better. On e-SNLI natural language inference, with about 98k parameters outside the embedding, the model reaches $76.98 \pm 0.17$% test accuracy, level with a softmax transformer of the same size ($76.62 \pm 0.36$%). Deleting the word its evidence ranks first changes the answer in 45% of test pairs, out of the 53% any single deletion can change, against 32% for the softmax model explained the same way and 40% by its attention x gradient. Attention can look as much like the words annotators highlighted as the evidence does, yet accounts for the answer less well: deleting the word it ranks first changes the Born Transformer's answer in 32% of pairs. The same weights compile exactly to optoelectronic optics and to qubits, and a coherent attention layer becomes one circuit equal to the model (852 CNOTs on 23 qubits). On IBM's ibm_kingston, reading only the attention overlaps by Hadamard tests, the device gave the model's answers, also when a word was deleted. With calibration circuits as deep as the overlaps, each word's evidence with the device's attention row sums followed the exact evidence (correlations 0.997 and 0.932 on two pairs chosen in advance); where a pair's evidence is a small total of large opposite terms the earlier runs say it does not, and we say why.
item.dc:creator: Teerawat Tongloy, Jiraporn Pongsopa, Rangsan Jomtarak
